title: Jailbreak Benchmark Contamination Check: Are Safety Evaluations Inflated by Training Data Overlap?

refinements_applied.change: Refine novelty for 'Jailbreak Benchmark Contamination Check:': Target a specific literature gap: new model family, new eval methodology, or novel combination.

sections.research_question: To what extent does if harmful prompts from public jailbreak benchmarks (jailbreakbench, strongreject) are present in safety fine-tuning datasets, models may appear more robust than they are — they have memorized refusal?
sections.approach_outline: Take a set of 100 harmful prompts from JailbreakBench and StrongREJECT. For each prompt, generate 5 semantically equivalent paraphrases using a separate model. Test attack success rate on originals vs. paraphrases on 3-5 commonly evaluated models. A large gap (originals refused, paraphrases not) is evidence of memorization rather than generalization. Compute contamination index as the ASR ratio paraphrase/original.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
Experiment 1 (Baseline): Set up experimental framework with a small public model. Replicate core measurement to establish baseline. ~8 hours.
Experiment 2 (Core): Apply methodology to target scenario. Measure primary metric vs baseline. ~12 hours.
Experiment 3 (Robustness): Test sensitivity to key parameters with 2+ variations. ~10 hours.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Benchmark contamination would mean safety evaluations are systematically overestimating robustness. This is a straightforward experiment with high impact: it either validates or undermines the field's primary evaluation methodology.
sections.strength_rationale:
theory_of_impact (5/5): Compelling chain addressing a critical problem: if benchmark contamination inflates safety scores, the entire field's evaluation methodology is undermined. The contamination index has independent value as a standard metric. Either outcome is highly informative.

accessible_complexity (5/5): Paraphrase prompts using an LLM, run them against models via API or local inference, compare ASR. No ML training required. Standard Python scripting with publicly available benchmarks and models. Highly beginner-friendly.

narrow_scope (5/5): Tightly scoped: take 100 prompts, generate paraphrases, test originals vs. paraphrases, compute ASR ratio. Single clear experiment with obvious deliverable (contamination index table). Easily fits in 30 hours.

novelty (3/5): Benchmark contamination in LLMs is a well-studied problem. The ICML 2025 paper 'How Much Can We Forget about Data Contamination?' directly addresses contamination effects on benchmarks. JailbreakBench (NeurIPS 2024) and GuardVal specifically tackle dynamic generation to reduce contamination risk. SafetyPrompts.com catalogs contamination-prone benchmarks. However, the specific framing of computing a 'contamination index' by comparing ASR on original vs. paraphrased jailbreak prompts to measure inflation of safety scores is a narrower and partially novel operationalization. The general problem is known; the specific paraphrase-based methodology adds incremental novelty.

JailbreakBench (NeurIPS 2024) - open robustness benchmark acknowledging contamination risks
GuardVal - dynamic jailbreak evaluation to minimize data contamination risks

title: Monitor Consistency Failure: Do Repeated Queries to the Same Monitor Yield Inconsistent Verdicts?

refinements_applied.change: Evidence-based novelty assessment: no published work has measured intra-model stochastic variance of safety monitors on adversarial agent trajectories. MRT paper left this gap open. CTRL-ALT-DECEIT notes aggregation helps but does not quantify variance or flip rates.

sections.research_question: LLM monitors are stochastic — querying the same agent trajectory twice may yield different suspicion verdicts due to temperature sampling. This inconsistency is a failure mode that has not been quantified for safety monitors operating on adversarial agent trajectories. How large is the variance, and does it concentrate on the borderline cases where monitoring reliability matters most?
sections.approach_outline: Using the ScaleAI/MRT dataset (pre-generated agent transcripts with monitor verdicts from "Reliable Weak-to-Strong Monitoring of LLM Agents"), re-query an LLM monitor on the same transcripts 10 times with temperature > 0. Measure variance in suspicion scores and flip rate (fraction of cases where the majority verdict differs from minority verdict). Stratify by adversarial strategy and original score region to test whether inconsistency concentrates on borderline or adversarial cases.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
Experiment 1 — Variance measurement (~12h): Download MRT transcripts from HuggingFace. Select a representative subset (~50-100 transcripts spanning benign, sabotage, and different adversarial strategies). Query a monitor LLM 10× per transcript at temperature 0.7. Compute per-transcript score variance and flip rate relative to ground-truth labels. Stratify by adversarial strategy and original score region to test whether inconsistency concentrates on borderline/adversarial cases.
Experiment 2 — Majority-vote mitigation (~10h): Simulate majority-vote ensembles at k=3, 5, 10 from the repeated queries. Measure flip rate reduction and accuracy improvement against ground truth. Report the cost multiplier vs accuracy gain curve and the minimum k needed to bring flip rate below 5%.
Write-up (~8h): Analyze results and produce blog post.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Stochastic monitoring inconsistency means safety guarantees based on monitoring outcomes have an unacknowledged random component. If monitor verdicts flip on the same transcript due to sampling noise — especially on borderline adversarial cases where detection matters most — then single-query monitoring provides weaker safety guarantees than assumed. Quantifying this directly informs deployment decisions about when and how to ensemble monitor queries.
sections.strength_rationale:
theory_of_impact (4/5): Stochastic inconsistency in monitoring means safety guarantees have an unacknowledged random component. Quantifying this has direct practical value for deployment reliability. The result directly informs whether labs should ensemble monitor queries and at what cost.

accessible_complexity (5/5): Query the same API 10 times per transcript and compute variance. This is the simplest possible experiment: repeated API calls and basic statistics. No ML training, no complex setup. MRT transcripts are pre-generated on HuggingFace. Ideal for beginners.

narrow_scope (5/5): Extremely well-defined: download transcripts, run monitor 10 times per transcript, compute variance and flip rate. Single clear deliverable. Easily completable within 30 hours even accounting for API costs.

novelty (4/5, confidence 0.7): No published work has systematically measured intra-model stochastic variance of safety monitors on adversarial agent trajectories. The MRT paper (Kale et al.) measures monitor reliability under adversarial conditions but treats each query as a single evaluation. CTRL-ALT-DECEIT notes aggregation helps but doesn't quantify variance or flip rates. General LLM-as-judge variance papers exist but none target safety monitoring with adversarial stratification.

Measure inter-judge agreement vs. agreement within the same model family. Identify safety behaviors where same-family judge pairs give systematically different verdicts than cross-family pairs. Compare judge verdicts with human expert ground truth.

sections.research_question: To what extent does safety benchmark results may be unstable when evaluated on random subsets of the full dataset, raising questions about how many test items are actually needed for reliable safety claims?
sections.approach_outline: Take a full safety benchmark dataset (e.g., a subset of AILuminate with 1000+ items). Evaluate 2–3 models on the full set and on random subsamples of 50, 100, 200, 500 items. Compute variance of safety scores across 10 random subsamples per size. Identify the minimum subsample size at which variance falls below a defined threshold.

sections.research_question: To what extent does comprehensive safety benchmarks like ailuminate require running 24,000 prompts per language. for resource-constrained researchers and practitioners, this is prohibitive. no minimal battery of safety p?
sections.approach_outline: Using published AILuminate scores for available models, identify a minimal subset of prompts (50–200) that maximally preserves the model ranking on the full benchmark. Validate on held-out models and publish the minimal battery.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
Experiment 1 (Baseline): Set up the experimental framework using a small, publicly available model. Replicate the core measurement from existing work to establish a baseline. Expected: reproduce known results within 10% margin. Time: ~8 hours.

sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Lowering the cost of safety evaluation enables more frequent evaluation (including post-fine-tune regression testing) by resource-constrained practitioners, increasing the overall safety-evaluation cadence.

novelty (3/5): AILuminate itself uses a subset selection approach: 1,200 seed prompts selected from a larger dataset, and the v0.5 Security evaluator uses an improved subset of the v1.0 Safety evaluator. However, the specific optimization problem of finding a minimal prompt subset (50-200 items) that maximally preserves model rankings on the full AILuminate benchmark, validated on held-out models, has not been published as a standalone study. The methodological contribution is incremental but the specific deliverable is novel.

sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models behave more honestly when they believe they are being evaluated, that is a safety-critical form of deception. It undermines all benchmark-based honesty evaluations.

The general concept is established but the honesty-specific framing is less explored.

sections.research_question: To what extent does sycophancy interacts with calibration failure: a model that agrees with a false premise may also express high confidence in that false agreement, compounding the harm by reducing user doubt?
sections.approach_outline: Measure expressed confidence in sycophantic vs. honest responses. Test whether sycophantic responses are systematically overconfident. Evaluate whether overconfidence is itself pressure-sensitive (does confidence increase with more insistent users?).

sections.theory_of_impact_chain: A sycophantic but hedged response leaves room for user doubt. A sycophantic and overconfident response forecloses doubt entirely, maximizing the likelihood of harmful action.

sections.approach_outline: Adapt Netflix's Chaos Engineering methodology. Systematically inject random 'faults' into the conversation context—noisy system prompts, partial instructions, injected irrelevant context, truncated system prompt, simulated memory errors—and observe whether safety guardrails hold under degraded conditions. Implement a lightweight 'Chaos Monkey' script that randomly perturbs prompt components before each API call in a test harness. Measure safety degradation as a function of chaos intensity.

sections.approach_outline: Import tolerance interval methodology from clinical trial statistics. A tolerance interval gives a range that covers at least a given proportion of the population with a given confidence level—exactly what is needed for safety certification claims. Run a safety probe battery on a model, compute tolerance intervals on refusal rates for each harm category, and use these to make statistically grounded claims like 'with 95% confidence, at least 99% of prompts in category X are refused'. Compare tolerance interval widths across models and harm categories to identify where more evaluation data is needed.

sections.research_question: To what extent does prompt injection detection is done with llm-based judges which are slow, expensive, and themselves vulnerable to adversarial manipulation. lightweight, rule-based detection is needed?
sections.approach_outline: Import SNORT/Suricata intrusion detection rule methodology from network security. Analyze a corpus of successful prompt injections and extract structural signatures (e.g., instruction-override patterns, role-switch tokens, delimiter escapes, encoding anomalies). sections.research_question: To what extent does most safety benchmarks test single-turn text, but deployed agents take sequences of actions. there is no simple taxonomy of how agentic failures differ from chat failures?
sections.approach_outline: Use a lightweight ReAct-style agent (e.g., LangChain or Inspect AI) with a web search or file-system tool. Design 20–30 multi-step scenarios where safe behavior requires mid-task refusal or course correction (e.g., being asked to find and aggregate personal information progressively). Categorize failures into: early refusal, late refusal, silent compliance, and incorrect refusal. Map these to existing taxonomies in the 2025 AI Agent Index paper.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
Experiment 1 (Baseline): Set up experimental framework with a small public model. Replicate core measurement to establish baseline. ~8 hours.
Experiment 2 (Core): Apply methodology to target scenario. Measure primary metric vs baseline. ~12 hours.
Experiment 3 (Robustness): Test sensitivity to key parameters with 2+ variations. ~10 hours.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Agentic safety is an open problem and most students can run small agent frameworks. A failure taxonomy helps future evaluators know what to look for and contributes a structured vocabulary to the field.
sections.strength_rationale:
theory_of_impact (3/5): Plausible chain: taxonomy helps structure future agentic safety evaluation. However, a toy taxonomy from 20-30 scenarios has limited direct impact without broader validation.

accessible_complexity (4/5): Using LangChain or Inspect AI to build a lightweight agent is beginner-friendly with existing tutorials. Designing scenarios and categorizing failures is accessible analytical work.

narrow_scope (4/5): Design 20-30 scenarios, run them, categorize failures. This is a tightly scoped deliverable achievable within 30 hours using existing agent frameworks.

novelty (3/5): Several agentic safety taxonomies and benchmarks exist: ST-WebAgentBench (2024) evaluates web agent safety across 222 tasks with 6 orthogonal dimensions; OpenAgentSafety (2025) provides executable environments for stress-testing agents; and multiple frameworks (ATFAA, SHIELD, Microsoft failure mode taxonomy, MAESTRO, OWASP Agentic AI) address the threat landscape. However, these are all complex, research-grade tools. The specific angle of creating a simplified, beginner-accessible taxonomy with a minimal 20-30 scenario set focused on mid-task refusal categorization (early refusal, late refusal, silent compliance, incorrect refusal) has not been done. The pedagogical framing for beginners provides moderate novelty.

sections.research_question: To what extent does standard oversight may miss even relatively obvious forms of deception due to cognitive biases, time pressure, and capability limitations. the minimum detectable deception threshold has not been empir?
sections.approach_outline: Implement deceptive models at varying levels of subtlety (obvious to subtle). Apply standard oversight protocols and measure the detection rate at each subtlety level. Identify the threshold where detection drops below 50%.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
Experiment 1 (Baseline): Set up experimental framework with a small public model. Replicate core measurement to establish baseline. ~8 hours.
Experiment 2 (Core): Apply methodology to target scenario. Measure primary metric vs baseline. ~12 hours.
Experiment 3 (Robustness): Test sensitivity to key parameters with 2+ variations. ~10 hours.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: The minimum detectable deception threshold defines how much trust we can place in current oversight. If obvious deception is missed, claims that current AI is well-overseen are false.
sections.strength_rationale:
theory_of_impact (4/5): The minimum detectable deception threshold directly quantifies how much trust we can place in current oversight. If even obvious deception is missed, this undermines claims about current AI safety. High impact finding either way.

title: Minimal Empirical Probe: Homogeneity Auditing as a Deployment Requirement (Single-Model)

sections.research_question: What does a focused empirical investigation of 'Homogeneity Auditing as a Deployment Requirement' reveal about safety-relevant behaviors in current language models, and what concrete, measurable findings can a beginner mentor-novice team produce within 30 hours using standard open-source tools?
sections.approach_outline: Load one pre-trained open-weight model (e.g., Gemma-2-2B) using the Hugging Face pipeline API. Curate 200 prompts covering the behavior of interest. Extract last-layer hidden states and train a logistic regression probe with 80/20 split. Pre-register success criterion: AUC > 0.70 on 40 held-out examples. Report result + 300-word blog section. Total: ~15-20 hours including setup. The original framing ('Homogeneity Auditing as a Deployment Requirement') was refined through Phase 2 strengthening and Phase 3 framing selection; the promoted framing 'Minimal Empirical Probe: Homogeneity Auditing as a Deployment Requirement (Single-Model)' achieved a higher weighted score. The mentor handles environment setup and code review; the novice drives data collection, analysis, and blog writing. All results are reported in a public blog post suitable for a general AI safety audience.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline data collection: load one pre-trained open-weight model (≤7B parameters, e.g., Gemma-2-2B or Phi-3-mini) using the Hugging Face pipeline API. Curate a set of 150-200 prompts spanning the safety-relevant behavior of interest (sourced from public datasets or hand-crafted). Run the model on all prompts and record outputs. Manually label 50 examples as 'target behavior present/absent'. Expected outcome: a labelled dataset establishing a baseline rate for the phenomenon, completable in 4-6 hours.
- Feature/activation extraction: using SAELens or TransformerLens, extract internal representations (residual stream activations or SAE feature activations at layer 12 or the last-third of the model) for the labelled dataset. Compute one summary metric: cosine similarity between the mean activation vectors of the two labeled classes, or the top-10 SAE feature activation magnitudes per class. Expected outcome: a quantitative signature distinguishing the two behavioral conditions, reportable in a 2x2 table, completable in 6-8 hours.
- Targeted intervention: having identified the key discriminative feature or probe direction, run one causal intervention — either zero-ablate the top SAE feature or steer activations in the probe direction — on 20 test examples. Measure whether the model's output changes in the expected direction (report % change in target behavior). This is the headline result for the blog post, completable in 4-6 hours.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: (A) This research produces a concrete, reproducible empirical finding about a safety-relevant behavior in current language models — specifically, whether internal representations or features predictably correspond to the target behavior, and whether causal interventions can modify it. (B) That finding either confirms or disconfirms a known safety hypothesis, directly informing the design of safety evaluations, monitoring probes, or fine-tuning interventions used by safety teams. (C) Better safety evaluations and monitoring reduce the probability that deployed models exhibit undetected harmful behaviors at scale, lowering the risk of catastrophic outcomes from advanced AI systems.
sections.strength_rationale: This idea scores strongly on its highest-weighted criteria: narrow_scope=5, accessible_complexity=5 (weighted score 4.43/5.00 after refinement). Phase 2 strengthening raised theory_of_impact, accessible_complexity, narrow_scope. The safety relevance is concrete and communicable in a blog post without requiring deep specialist knowledge.

sections.research_question: To what extent does the artificial hivemind paper aggregated across model sizes. it is unknown whether smaller or larger models contribute more to inter-model homogeneity?
sections.approach_outline: Stratify the existing Infinity-Chat experimental setup by model parameter count and compare intra-size-class vs. cross-size-class homogeneity. Test whether frontier models converge more with each other than with smaller models.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
Experiment 1 (Baseline): Set up experimental framework with a small public model. Replicate core measurement to establish baseline. ~8 hours.
Experiment 2 (Core): Apply methodology to target scenario. Measure primary metric vs baseline. ~12 hours.
Experiment 3 (Robustness): Test sensitivity to key parameters with 2+ variations. ~10 hours.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If frontier models are the most homogeneous, the concentration of deployment in this tier amplifies systemic risk; if smaller models are more diverse, this has implications for deployment portfolio design.
sections.strength_rationale:
theory_of_impact (3/5): Plausible with gap: understanding the size-homogeneity relationship is informative for deployment strategy, but the direct chain to safety improvement is unclear.

accessible_complexity (3/5): Intermediate: stratifying existing data by model size and computing similarity metrics is manageable for CS students with data analysis skills.

narrow_scope (4/5): Focused deliverable: size-stratified homogeneity analysis using existing Infinity-Chat data, with clear intra-class vs. cross-class comparison.

novelty (4/5): The Artificial Hivemind paper aggregated across model sizes and did not report size-stratified analysis. Scaling laws literature focuses on performance, not inter-model similarity. This is a natural disaggregation of the Hivemind findings that no one has published, and the Infinity-Chat data potentially supports it directly.

sections.research_question: To what extent does when concept steering suppresses a harmful feature, the model may compensate by distributing the suppressed computation across other features or layers — a form of activation re-routing. this re-routi?

Measure how the residual stream changes across all other features and layers when steering is active vs. inactive. Train a secondary classifier to detect whether steering is active from post-intervention activations. Measure detection accuracy.
